passage:
Dear Mr. Davis,

When our kitchen remodeling project started on February 15th, I hired your company because of your great reputation for reliability. However, after I paid the $12,500 deposit, which is half of the total contract price, all work at my house on 42 Oakridge Lane completely stopped for no good reason. I am writing to send a final notice about your team's ongoing absence from the job site.

As of today, March 31st, none of your workers have shown up at my property for twenty-one business days in a row. My biggest concern is the dangerous condition in which the room was left. The main floor is still torn apart, with exposed electrical wires and open plumbing pipes that were supposed to be checked three weeks ago. Leaving a job half-finished like this has made my home unlivable for my family. It has also messed up the schedules of the flooring and cabinet installers I hired based on your original timeline.

Also, my phone calls and emails to you have been completely ignored. While I know that construction companies sometimes face supply delays, failing to communicate with a customer is completely unprofessional. According to Section 4 of our signed agreement, stopping work for more than ten days without a valid reason breaks our contract.

I am asking you to restart the work and send me an updated project schedule by 9:00 AM this Friday, April 3rd. If your workers do not show up on-site or if you fail to give a clear explanation for this delay, I will have no choice but to cancel our contract. In that case, I will take legal steps to get back the unused portion of my deposit and report your business to the provincial licensing board.

I expect to hear back from you immediately confirming when your crew will return to finish the job.

Sincerely,
Julian Vance
